newsitem.title: GERMANY: German tax talks collapse amid recriminations.
newsitem.headline: German tax talks collapse amid recriminations.

text.p: Talks on tax reforms between the ruling German coalition and Social Democrat (SPD) opposition collapsed on Wednesday, opening the way for a bruising parliamentary battle which could run into the 1998 election campaign.
The talks on Finance Minister Theo Waigel's package of 30 billion marks ($17.5 billion) in tax cuts broke off after just an hour with both sides blaming each other.
"The SPD was not able to agree to our planned tax cuts and pensions reforms," Waigel told reporters. "The SPD wants to cut occupational insurance charges by just redistributing wealth."
SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine hit back that the government had flatly refused its call to link tax reforms to cutting the charges in a bid to battle high German unemployment.

The talks had been an attempt to reach a compromise to pre-empt months of wrangling in the German parliament, where Chancellor Helmut Kohl controls the Bundestag lower house but the SPD rules in the second chamber, the Bundesrat.

The two sides had come close to agreeing to cut the bottom rate of income tax and reduce corporation tax but the main sticking point was Waigel's plan to cut the top rate of income tax to 39 percent in 1999 from 53 percent.
The SPD also fundamentally opposed the government's Anglo-Saxon-style supply-side approach of cutting taxes to encouraging corporate investment.
It demanded above all that a big reduction in non-wage labour costs -- unemployment, health and pensions insurance charges -- be made this summer to boost consumer demand.
Chances of a breakthrough had already dived this week after a testy exchange of letters between Kohl and Lafontaine in which both refused to concede any ground.

Independent analysts said the breakdown came as no great surprise but added that continuing uncertainty would not help nurture economic recovery as Bonn struggles to contain borrowing to qualify for the European single currency.
"I would have been very surprised if there had been a breakthrough in these talks today," said Holger Fahrinkrug, an economist at UBS in Frankfurt.
"The government will continue to try to push this through the legislative process but the chances are very slim indeed that the reform will come through as it stands."
Lafontaine vowed to fight the government tax plan. "We will not have a tax lie on the statute books in 1999," he said after the talks in the federal chancellery.
"It is a reform against the people and the economy."

But coalition leaders said they had wasted no time in their bid to move legislation through Bonn's cumbersome parliamentary process and said the tax debate would be settled in regional polls running up to the October 1998 national vote.

"The voters in Hamburg, Lower Saxony and Saxony-Anhalt have the power to break the SPD blockade in the forthcoming state elections," Peter Hintze, general secretary of Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) said in a statement. All three are SPD-led and form part of the opposition majority in the Bundesrat.

Waigel's 1998 tax bill has already had its first reading in the lower house. A bill for 1999, to make the lion's share of income and corporate tax cuts, was approved by Kohl's team on Tuesday and will have its first reading on Friday.
"The government is absolutely determined to push ahead with its policies. We cannot come to a standstill," he said.
Waigel said both measures should clear the lower house before the summer holidays and both sides said the Bundesrat would also address the bills before the recess.
If the SPD makes good on its promise to oppose the bills in the Bundesrat, then the two sides would face each other again when parliament's mediation committee is convened this summer.
Politicians had earlier said mediation efforts would not start until September.

SPD parliamentary leader Rudolf Scharping said he would now initiate legislation to cut unemployment, health and pensions insurance contributions by a gross 30 billion marks in 1998. He said the net relief to companies and workers would be between seven and 10 billion marks.
-- Bonn newsroom, 49-228-26097 150 ($ = 1.712 German Marks)
